newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia pay-TV shake-up plan seen good for all.
newsitem.headline: Australia pay-TV shake-up plan seen good for all.

text.p: The pact between Australia's key media players to rationalise the loss-making pay television industry would be good for all players ans investors in the pay TV sector, analysts said on Monday.
Kerry Packer's Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd (PBL), Rupert Murdoch's News Corp Ltd and its cable TV partner Telstra Corp Ltd agreed on Friday to rationalise the pay-TV sector.
"I think it will be good for everyone," said one Sydney based media analyst, who did not want to be named.

PBL has about an 11 percent economic interest in cash strapped satellite TV operator Australis Media Ltd and has agreed to sell the Australis bonds it holds to News Corp and Telstra, but intends to retain its Australis shares.

Analysts said this transaction could be the first step to a Foxtel/Australis merger. However this is not a certainty as the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) knocked back a Foxtel/Australis merger proposal in November 1995.
A Foxtel spokesman said it was premature to speculate about a merger. The ACCC were unavailable for comment.

Australis is seen as the most vulnerable to takeover of Australia's three major pay-TV players due to its weak financial position. The third player Optus Vision is owned by telephone carrier Optus Communications Pty Ltd.
However, the key phrase from Friday's statement was "PBL will be given the opportunity to equalise its interests in pay-TV with News interests."
Analysts said this could mean that PBL would be able to buy into an enlarged Foxtel-Australis, if a merger went ahead.
Foxtel is jointly owned by News Corp and state-owned Telstra, which is due to offer a third of its shares as part of a share market float later this year.
Analysts said Telstra would be looking to reduce its exposure to pay-TV head of its proposed float.

"This is all related to the Telstra float and it also means there are separate negotiations between Telstra and News Corp over the (cable) rollout and I gather News Corp will receive some sort of cash payment for that as well," one analyst said.

Recent media reports said Telstra planned to cut back the rollout of its A$3 billion cable network as part of a pre-float cost cutting exercise, which would also result in a compensation payment to News Corp over their rollout agreement.
If an Australis/Foxtel merger went ahead Australis satellite and microwave coverage would cover most of the country, thereby reducing the need for an extensive cable network rollout.

The key asset of Australis is its progamming arrangement with Foxtel, which has agreed to pay Australis A$4.5 billion over 25 years to supply programming to Foxtel. Analysts said Foxtel would be keen to untangle itself from this deal.

An Australis spokesman said it would have to be involved in any industry rationalisation, but would not comment any further. Australis is currently appealling against a ruling by the Supreme Court of New South Wales (NSW) that blocked a proposed satellite merger with Optus Vision.
Analysts said Optus Vision is not out of the picture yet.
"It does not rule them out of the equation, but it makes life very difficult for them," the Melbourne analyst said.
Optus Vision said it was not making any comment.

A shake-out in Australia's pay-TV industry has been long awaited. The industry has lost more than A$1.5 billion since 1993, and caused the delays of the planned Optus Communications float and could hamper the Telstra float.

Investors reacted favourably to Friday's annoucement. At 3.05 p.m. (0505 GMT) PBL shares were up 16 cents to A$7.50. Australis shares topped the turnover lists with 11.8 million shares traded with its shares up two cents to 14 cents.
-- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
